shipped_rows.title_o: Handedness and behavioural inhibition: Left-handed females show most inhibition as measured by BIS/BAS self-report

blind_target.title: Differences between left- and right-handers in approach/avoidance motivation: influence of consistency of handedness measures.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Our results replicate those of Wright et al. (2009) and Hardie and Wright (2014) that left-handers have higher BIS scores than right-handers while, as expected, there is no handedness difference for any BAS sub-scale.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Hardie and Wright (2014), using the type of classification scheme advocated by Prichard et al. (2013) and a number of different cut-off values to define consistent versus inconsistent handedness, found small but statistically significant effects of consistency or strength of handedness for their sample (N=689) as a whole (consistently handed individuals had higher BIS scores than those of inconsistent handedness). However, when they looked separately at right-handers and left- handers an effect was apparent among the 202 left-handers but not among 481 right-handers. Our own failure to find an effect of strength of handedness may, therefore, be a consequence of the relatively low number of left-handers (36) in our sample.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Direction finding confirmed; strength finding differs for Hardie and Wright. Wright et al. has an explicit overall replication verdict.

luna_triage.reason: The paper explicitly says its results replicate Hardie and Wright (2014)'s finding that left-handers have higher BIS scores. Its full reference list gives that distinct 2014 work and DOI. The only supplied shipped original is Wright, Hardie, and Wilson (2009), a different cited paper and not a representation of the 2014 work.
